text: Before you write a single query, plan the architecture. Both stakeholders' requirement lists from Lesson 1 point to the same underlying numbers, which is the tell that this is one data model serving two report pages, not two separate reports built from scratch.

The single most important decision is grain: what does one row of your fact table represent? Here it has to be the order line, not the order. Sales dot SalesOrderDetail already gives you one row per product per order, with LineTotal pre-calculated correctly. Aggregate up to the order level first, and you lose the ability to slice by product, which is exactly what the Operations Manager asked for.

So the architecture is a small, deliberate star: one fact table at order-line grain, with keys plus OrderQty and LineTotal. Two small dimension tables, Product and Territory, carrying the descriptive names. And a Date table, marked as the model's official date table, because DAX time intelligence in Lesson 6 needs one.

Here's the detail that matters: the fact view carries TerritoryID and ProductID, not TerritoryName and ProductName. The names live only in the dimension views. That's what makes the relationships you'll build in Lesson 5 real relationships the model actually uses, not just decoration sitting next to a flat table.

This is also exactly why this project can't reuse the Beginner project's one giant flat query. Two pages need different slices of the same facts, and a flat, pre-joined result can't support that cleanly. Next lesson: turning this architecture into a real, multi-table T-SQL query against AdventureWorks2012.
